title: Why does every button print quit?
blurb: Predict what a loop of lambdas prints, explain it, then fix it two ways.

brief.why: Uses Functions are objects and Closures: predict, then explain in your own words.

tryit.question_md:
Predict first, then explain. What does this print?

```python
buttons = []
for label in ["save", "load", "quit"]:
    buttons.append(lambda: print(label))

for press in buttons:
    press()
```

Say **why**, in terms of what each lambda keeps hold of. Then fix it **two different ways** so each button prints its own label, and say *when* each fix captures the label.
tryit.model_md:
It prints `quit` three times.

Each lambda is a function object stored in the list. It does not keep the value of `label`: it keeps the variable itself (a closure over the loop variable), and it looks `label` up only when it is called. By the time the buttons are pressed the loop has ended, so the one shared variable holds `"quit"` for every lambda.

Fix 1, a default argument: `lambda label=label: print(label)`. A default is evaluated when the lambda is defined, so it stores the current value of `label` on each pass of the loop.

Fix 2, a factory function: `def make(text): return lambda: print(text)` and `buttons.append(make(label))`. Each call of the factory creates a new scope with its own `text`, so each returned lambda closes over its own label. The value is captured when the factory is called, during the loop.

rubric.text: Predicts that it prints quit three times.
Explains that each lambda keeps the variable label, not its value, and looks it up only when called, after the loop has ended.
Fixes it with a default argument (lambda label=label), which stores the current value when the lambda is defined.
Fixes it a second way with a factory function whose new scope holds its own label for each returned lambda.
